README.md:25:### Setting up virtual environment (recommended)
README.md:26:
README.md:27:We strongly recommend creating a virtual Python environment for everybody
README.md:28:working with more than one Python project (this includes even using both
README.md:29:Postgkyl and Sphinx). The two recommended options are
README.md:30:[venv](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) and
README.md:31:[mamba](https://mamba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).
README.md:32:
README.md:33:With `venv`, one can create the virtual environment with:
README.md:34:
README.md:35:```bash
README.md:36:python -m venv /path/to/new/virtual/environments/pgkyl
README.md:37:```
README.md:38:
README.md:39:then activate it with:
README.md:40:
README.md:41:| bash/zsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate`      |
README.md:42:| fish     | `source <venv>/bin/activate.fish` |
README.md:43:| csh/tcsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate.csh`  |
README.md:44:
README.md:45:and deactivate with:
README.md:46:
README.md:47:```bash
README.md:48:deactivate
README.md:49:```
README.md:50:
README.md:51:With `mamba`, one can create the virtual environment with:
README.md:52:
README.md:53:```bash
README.md:54:mamba create -n pgkyl
README.md:55:```
README.md:56:
README.md:57:then activate with:
README.md:58:
README.md:59:```bash
README.md:60:mamba activate pgkyl
README.md:61:```
README.md:62:
README.md:63:and deactivate with:
README.md:64:
README.md:65:```bash
README.md:66:mamba deactivate
README.md:67:```
README.md:68:
README.md:69:Note that with `mamba`, one can also use the provided `environment.yml` file,
README.md:70:which also includes dependency specifications:
README.md:71:
README.md:72:```bash
README.md:73:mamba env create -f environment.yml
README.md:74:```
README.md:75:
README.md:76:### Installing Postgkyl
README.md:77:
README.md:78:The Postgkyl itself is installed with `pip`.[^1] Developers and uses who want to
README.md:79:have the most up-to-date version should install Postgkyl from the source code:
README.md:80:
README.md:81:```bash
README.md:82:git clone https://github.com/ammarhakim/postgkyl.git
README.md:83:cd postgkyl
README.md:84:pip install --upgrade numpy setuptools wheel
README.md:85:pip install -e '.[test]' --no-build-isolation
README.md:86:```
README.md:87:
README.md:88:Alternatively, Postgkyl can be installed directly from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/postgkyl/):
README.md:89:
README.md:90:```bash
README.md:91:pip install --upgrade numpy setuptools wheel
README.md:92:pip install -e postgkyl[test] --no-build-isolation
README.md:93:```
README.md:94:
README.md:95:#### The Gkeyll bridge (native `.gkyl` reading, `interpolate`, weak algebra)
README.md:96:
README.md:97:Postgkyl talks to Gkeyll through a small compiled bridge (`gpython`), not a path you configure. **This is
README.md:98:built automatically** as part of `pip install`/`pip install -e .`. `setup.py` runs
README.md:99:`scripts/build_gkeyll.sh`, which:
README.md:100:
README.md:101:1. clones [Gkeyll](https://github.com/ammarhakim/gkeyll) into `./gkeyll/`
README.md:102:   (a sparse, blobless, depth-1 clone of just the `core/` app — a few tens
README.md:103:   of MB, not a submodule),
README.md:104:2. `./configure`s and `make core`s it into `gkeyll/build/core/libg0core.so`
README.md:105:   with no external dependencies (`--use-lapack-lite=yes`, so no
README.md:106:   MPI/CUDA/SuperLU/Lua/system LAPACK are required), then
README.md:107:3. compiles postgkyl's `_gpython` CPython extension
README.md:108:   (`src/postgkyl/gpython/csrc/_gpythonmodule.c`) against it.
README.md:109:
README.md:110:This step needs **network access** (to clone Gkeyll) and **a C compiler**.
README.md:111:It defaults to `cc`; if your system doesn't have `cc`, set `CC=gcc` (or any compiler you have) before
README.md:112:installing:
README.md:113:```bash
README.md:114:CC=gcc pip install -e '.[test]' --no-build-isolation
README.md:115:```
README.md:116:
README.md:117:**Always install with `--no-build-isolation`** (as above). Without it, `pip`
README.md:118:builds the extension in a throwaway environment that resolves `numpy`
README.md:119:independently of the one that ends up installed for running Postgkyl. The
README.md:120:extension targets NumPy's `>=2.2` ABI explicitly (matching the `numpy>=2.2.6`
README.md:121:floor above) so that a same-major mismatch fails loudly at import with a clear
README.md:122:`numpy.dtype size changed` error rather than silently — but this is a
README.md:123:best-effort backstop, not a guarantee: a build/runtime NumPy skew has been
README.md:124:observed to crash the native bridge outright (segfault or memory corruption
README.md:125:inside Gkeyll's own C code, surfacing anywhere from the next file read to an
README.md:126:unrelated `matplotlib` call much later) instead of raising cleanly. Building
README.md:127:against the exact NumPy already installed is the only reliable fix, which is
README.md:128:what `--no-build-isolation` gives you.
README.md:129:
README.md:130:If this step fails or is skipped, Postgkyl still imports and works — reading
README.md:131:files falls back to a pure-Python reader, and anything that needs the
README.md:132:compiled bridge (`.interpolate()`, weak `* /` on modal data, native `.gkyl`
README.md:133:reading, `.integrate()`, …) raises a `RuntimeError` naming the missing piece
README.md:134:instead of the pipeline silently doing the wrong thing. Check whether the
README.md:135:bridge is active with:
README.md:136:```bash
README.md:137:python -c "from postgkyl import gpython; print(gpython.available())"
README.md:138:```
README.md:139:
README.md:140:To rebuild by hand (e.g. after pulling a Postgkyl or Gkeyll update, or after
README.md:141:fixing a compiler issue), re-run either script from the repo root — both are
README.md:142:safe to re-run:
README.md:143:```bash
README.md:144:scripts/build_gkeyll.sh   # full: re-clone/build libg0core.so, then the extension
README.md:145:scripts/build_gpython.sh  # just the extension, if libg0core.so is already built
README.md:146:```
README.md:147:
README.md:148:If `gpython.available()` is `False`, the printed error explains which of the
README.md:149:two prerequisites (compiler, or the clone) is missing, or whether the built
README.md:150:extension is stale relative to the shim header — the fix in that last case
README.md:151:is always `scripts/build_gpython.sh`.
README.md:152:
README.md:153:## Testing
README.md:154:
README.md:155:Postgkyl utilizes [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/) for testing. The tests can
README.md:156:be called manually from the root Postgkyl directory simply by using:
README.md:157:
README.md:158:```bash
README.md:159:pytest [-v]
README.md:160:```
README.md:161:
README.md:162:## API and CLI documentation
README.md:163:
README.md:164:Public command documentation lives on the Python function that implements the
README.md:165:operation. The equivalent `GData` spelling is a class-body alias to that same
README.md:166:function, so editor hover help, `help(pg.interpolate)`,
README.md:167:`help(data.interpolate)`, and `pgkyl interpolate --help` cannot maintain
README.md:168:separate descriptions.
README.md:169:The installed distribution includes a `py.typed` marker so language servers
README.md:170:consume these inline signatures and aliases from a virtual environment too.
README.md:171:
README.md:172:Command docstrings use `Args:` entries in Google style. Every CLI-visible
README.md:173:parameter needs one entry; command compilation rejects missing, duplicate, or
README.md:174:unknown parameter documentation. `tests/test_documentation.py` additionally
README.md:175:checks the public Python surface, static fluent aliases, source/runtime
README.md:176:docstring identity, and deterministic CLI lowering. Run it directly with:
README.md:177:
README.md:178:```bash
README.md:179:pytest tests/test_documentation.py
README.md:180:```

AGENTS.md:1:# Coding Doctrine
AGENTS.md:2:
AGENTS.md:3:**0. Locality of reasoning.** Every principle below is a projection of
AGENTS.md:4:one axiom: a reader must be able to understand a fragment without the
AGENTS.md:5:whole program. Whatever keeps a local conclusion sound — a frozen
AGENTS.md:6:record, an honest signature, a stated law — is doctrine. Whatever
AGENTS.md:7:forces a global search — ambient state, a leaky layer, a second copy
AGENTS.md:8:of a fact — is the enemy.
AGENTS.md:9:
AGENTS.md:10:*Data — what it does, and what it may say*
AGENTS.md:11:
AGENTS.md:12:**I. Data is inert. Functions transform.** No objects that know
AGENTS.md:13:things and do things. Data is a frozen record. Behavior is a function
AGENTS.md:14:that takes data in and returns data out. If you're reaching for
AGENTS.md:15:inheritance, you've taken a wrong turn.
AGENTS.md:16:
AGENTS.md:17:**II. Make illegal states unrepresentable.** The shape of a datum is
AGENTS.md:18:its strongest invariant. Constructors refuse invalid states; a checked
AGENTS.md:19:fact becomes a type; downstream never re-proves what upstream
AGENTS.md:20:established. Parse, don't validate.
AGENTS.md:21:
AGENTS.md:22:*Functions — one idea, honestly declared*
AGENTS.md:23:
AGENTS.md:24:**III. A function is one idea.** It takes exactly what it needs and
AGENTS.md:25:returns exactly what it computes. If the signature has two concepts in
AGENTS.md:26:it, you have two functions.
AGENTS.md:27:
AGENTS.md:28:**IV. The signature tells the whole truth.** Inward: if something
AGENTS.md:29:needs a value, it receives it as a parameter — no spooky action at a
AGENTS.md:30:distance, no stringly-typed interfaces, no implicit state. Outward:
AGENTS.md:31:same inputs, same outputs; effects and failure appear in the type, not
AGENTS.md:32:in the fine print. Pure core, effects at the edges.
AGENTS.md:33:
AGENTS.md:34:*Knowledge — one home per fact*
AGENTS.md:35:
AGENTS.md:36:**V. Every fact has one home.** One authoritative representation of
AGENTS.md:37:each decision and each piece of knowledge; everything else inherits or
AGENTS.md:38:is derived mechanically — never maintained by hand in parallel.
AGENTS.md:39:Configuration is decided once, at the highest level, and threaded
AGENTS.md:40:down; no module ever decides its own context. If the design and the
AGENTS.md:41:implementation can disagree, you have two sources of truth and zero.
AGENTS.md:42:
AGENTS.md:43:*Layers — what above, how below*
AGENTS.md:44:
AGENTS.md:45:**VI. Separate what from how.** Logic and machinery are different
AGENTS.md:46:concerns with a hard boundary. The layer that says *what* to compute
AGENTS.md:47:should be readable by someone who has never seen the machinery
AGENTS.md:48:underneath. The layer that says *how* lives below, stays below, and
AGENTS.md:49:nothing leaks up from it.
AGENTS.md:50:
AGENTS.md:51:**VII. Notation is execution; lowering is transliteration.** Looking
AGENTS.md:52:up: the spec layer reads like the math or logic it implements — when
AGENTS.md:53:notation *is* the executable object, not a comment beside it, bugs
AGENTS.md:54:have nowhere to hide. Looking down: the layer that executes the spec
AGENTS.md:55:reproduces it exactly — nothing added, nothing dropped, nothing
AGENTS.md:56:reinterpreted; no opinions, no defaults, no helpful conversions. If
AGENTS.md:57:the lowering changes anything, the spec is a lie.
AGENTS.md:58:
AGENTS.md:59:*Abstraction — earned, and binding*
AGENTS.md:60:
AGENTS.md:61:**VIII. Earn your abstractions.** No abstraction before the second
AGENTS.md:62:use. Three similar lines is better than a premature helper. The right
AGENTS.md:63:amount of complexity is the minimum the current task demands — not the
AGENTS.md:64:current task plus three hypothetical future ones.
AGENTS.md:65:
AGENTS.md:66:**IX. An abstraction is a contract.** It is defined by what it
AGENTS.md:67:guarantees, not what it hides. If you can't state what is always true
AGENTS.md:68:of it — properties a client may rely on without reading the
AGENTS.md:69:implementation — it isn't an abstraction, it's indirection. Two
AGENTS.md:70:implementations that honor the contract must be interchangeable; and
AGENTS.md:71:its outputs stay in its vocabulary, so uses compose.
AGENTS.md:72:
AGENTS.md:73:*Verification — formal first*
AGENTS.md:74:
AGENTS.md:75:**X. Trust the most formal thing first.** Types over tests, tests
AGENTS.md:76:over docs, docs over comments. Invest in whichever layer catches the
AGENTS.md:77:bug earliest with the least ongoing maintenance cost.
AGENTS.md:78:
AGENTS.md:79:## Commands
AGENTS.md:80:
AGENTS.md:81:```bash
AGENTS.md:82:# Install for development (editable) + test deps
AGENTS.md:83:pip install -e .[test]
AGENTS.md:84:
AGENTS.md:85:# Run the tests
AGENTS.md:86:pytest tests/
AGENTS.md:87:# Without an install, point Python at the src layout:
AGENTS.md:88:PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest tests/
AGENTS.md:89:
AGENTS.md:90:# Run the CLI (chained pipeline; mirrors the fluent script API)
AGENTS.md:91:pgkyl file.gkyl interpolate select --z0 0 plot
AGENTS.md:92:pgkyl file.gkyl info
AGENTS.md:93:
AGENTS.md:94:# A diagnostics chain (equation-specific physics; see diagnostics/)
AGENTS.md:95:# (diagnostics take NumPy-backed data, so interpolate always runs first)
AGENTS.md:96:pgkyl euler_5m_0.gkyl interpolate five-moment-pressure --num-moms 5 plot
AGENTS.md:97:
AGENTS.md:98:# An RPN chain over the working set (see operations/evaluate.py)
AGENTS.md:99:pgkyl a.gkyl b.gkyl evaluate "f0 f1 +" interpolate plot
AGENTS.md:100:
AGENTS.md:101:# `pgkyl --help` lists every registered command, grouped by section
AGENTS.md:102:# (Verbs / Diagnostics / Render / Utility).
AGENTS.md:103:pgkyl --help
AGENTS.md:104:pgkyl --version
AGENTS.md:105:```

AGENTS.md:107:## Architecture — a strict, one-way layered DAG
AGENTS.md:108:
AGENTS.md:109:Every folder has **one job**, and imports point in **one direction only** (leaves at the
AGENTS.md:110:bottom). There is **no import cycle** — this is enforced by a
AGENTS.md:111:test (see "Import contract"). Arrow = "may import":
AGENTS.md:112:

AGENTS.md:114:> mirror of `tests/test_postgkyl.py::_ALLOWED` — that dict (and the AST walk that checks
AGENTS.md:115:> every real import against it) is the enforced source of truth; this file is only a
AGENTS.md:116:> readable projection of it. The two *can* drift (they already had:
AGENTS.md:117:> `operations/average.py`, `operations/eval_at_coord_proj.py`, `operations/local_poly.py`,
AGENTS.md:118:> `gdatastate/guards.py`, `gdata/gdatagroup.py`, and `gdata/verbs.py` existed in the tree before they
AGENTS.md:119:> were added here). Whenever you add a new top-level module file or a new allowed import
AGENTS.md:120:> edge, update `_ALLOWED` and this section in the same commit — don't let the picture
AGENTS.md:121:> outlive the code it describes.

AGENTS.md:264:
AGENTS.md:265:### The two-domain lifecycle (REFACTOR_GKEYLL_FFI.md)
AGENTS.md:266:
AGENTS.md:267:Every dataset lives in one of two backends, discriminated by
AGENTS.md:268:`GDataState.backend`:
AGENTS.md:269:
AGENTS.md:270:- **`"gkyl"` (modal domain)** — DG coefficients as a native `gkyl_array`
AGENTS.md:271:  (`gpython.GkylArray`). Loading lands here. All math runs inside Gkeyll:
AGENTS.md:272:  `*`/`/` → weak kernels (`gkyl_dg_mul_op`/`div_op`), `+`/`-` → coefficient
AGENTS.md:273:  lin-combs (`gkyl_array_accumulate`), scalars → `scale`/mean-shift, integer
AGENTS.md:274:  powers → repeated weak multiply, `.integrate()` → `gkyl_array_integrate`.
AGENTS.md:275:  `values` is a read-only view; `np.asarray`/ufuncs/`select` refuse with
AGENTS.md:276:  ".interpolate() first".
AGENTS.md:277:- **`"numpy"` (field domain)** — post-`interpolate()` values as a plain ndarray;
AGENTS.md:278:  the unchanged NumPy stack (`select`, `plot`, ufuncs, arithmetic).
AGENTS.md:279:
AGENTS.md:280:`interpolate()` is the **one-way bridge**: matrix from Gkeyll's basis functions,
AGENTS.md:281:applied per cell with NumPy `tensordot`, returning a *new, by-value* array.
AGENTS.md:282:
AGENTS.md:283:Every dataset has one **`value_form`** (`ctx["value_form"]`): `modal`
AGENTS.md:284:coefficients, `nodal` values at the basis `node_list` points, or `quad`
AGENTS.md:285:values at Gauss–Legendre points. This is a single, backend-agnostic fact —
AGENTS.md:286:there is no separate `is_modal` flag duplicating it; a numpy-backed dataset
AGENTS.md:287:that was never native (e.g. a plain nodal-basis file read without the
AGENTS.md:288:Gkeyll library) carries the same three-valued `value_form` as a gkyl-native
AGENTS.md:289:one, and every consumer (`_require_operable`, `interpolate`, `average`, …)
AGENTS.md:290:reads that one key. **The capability boundary is modal vs point-values, not
AGENTS.md:291:gkyl vs NumPy:**
AGENTS.md:292:
AGENTS.md:293:- **modal** — only Gkeyll's DG operations: weak `* /`, coefficient `+ -`/scalar
AGENTS.md:294:  kernels, `.integrate()`, `.interpolate()`. Ufuncs/`np.asarray`/`plot` refuse.
AGENTS.md:295:- **nodal / quad** — the values ARE the field at points, so *every* pointwise
AGENTS.md:296:  NumPy operation is exact and allowed (ufuncs, `* / **`, `np.asarray`) —
AGENTS.md:297:  computed on the views, wrapped back native, **staying in-value_form** —
AGENTS.md:298:  and they `plot()` directly at their true point locations (non-tensor node
AGENTS.md:299:  sets, e.g. serendipity p2 in 2-D, plot via `.to_quad()`).
AGENTS.md:300:
AGENTS.md:301:Conversions are **never implicit** — only `.to_modal()/.to_nodal()/.to_quad()`
AGENTS.md:302:change `value_form` (nodal↔modal exact; quad round-trip exact for degree
AGENTS.md:303:≤ 2·num_quad−1); `.apply(fn, num_quad=…)` is the one-shot modal → quad → fn →
AGENTS.md:304:project-back spelling (≡ `fn(d.to_quad()).to_modal()`). Datasets combine only
AGENTS.md:305:within one value_form. See REFACTOR_GKEYLL_FFI.md §3b.
AGENTS.md:306:
AGENTS.md:307:`basis_type`, `poly_order`, and `value_form` are properties **of the data
AGENTS.md:308:itself** — read from a file's header metadata, or set once via `pg.load(...,
AGENTS.md:309:basis_type=..., poly_order=..., value_form=...)` / the CLI's bare-filename
AGENTS.md:310:`load` (`-b`/`-p`/`-v`) — never re-specified by a downstream verb. `.interpolate()`,
AGENTS.md:311:`.local_poly()`, `.average()`, `.eval_at_coord_proj()`, `.integrate()`, … all
AGENTS.md:312:read `ctx["basis_type"]`/`ctx["poly_order"]`/`ctx["value_form"]` off the
AGENTS.md:313:dataset and raise a clear error if a required one is missing; none of them
AGENTS.md:314:take a `basis`/`poly_order` override argument. Loading a dataset that has a
AGENTS.md:315:spatial grid (`ctx["cells"]`) without `basis_type`/`poly_order`/`value_form`
AGENTS.md:316:resolvable (neither in the file header nor given explicitly) warns and
AGENTS.md:317:defaults to `basis_type="serendipity"`, `poly_order=0`, `value_form="nodal"`
AGENTS.md:318:— the trivial one-point-per-cell basis, since there is no modal structure to
AGENTS.md:319:assume otherwise. When `value_form` is defaulted this way, the grid is
AGENTS.md:320:re-expressed as cell centers (p0 nodal's one point per cell) instead of the
AGENTS.md:321:reader's raw cell-edge grid, so it lines up one-to-one with `values`. A
AGENTS.md:322:dynvector/diagnostic file has no spatial grid and thus no DG basis to speak
AGENTS.md:323:of, so it is exempt from this defaulting. This is distinct from the readers'
AGENTS.md:324:own narrower default (`gkyl_c_reader.py`/`gkyl_reader.py`: `basis_type`
AGENTS.md:325:resolved but no `value_form` tag in the file -> assume `"modal"`, silently,
AGENTS.md:326:no warning) — there the data is *known* to be real DG output (the header
AGENTS.md:327:has a basis), so the stored numbers are almost certainly modal coefficients
AGENTS.md:328:already, not point values; that assumption is safe enough not to warn about.
AGENTS.md:329:The `gdatastate.py`-level default above only fires when nothing about a
AGENTS.md:330:basis was found at all.
AGENTS.md:331:
AGENTS.md:332:### `gdatastate/` — the container (`gdatastate/state.py`)
AGENTS.md:333:`GDataState` holds one dataset: a nodal `grid` (list of 1-D edge arrays), values in
AGENTS.md:334:one of the two backends (`gpython.GkylArray` or `np.ndarray`), and metadata in `ctx`.
AGENTS.md:335:It is **verb-less** and imports only downward (`io` to construct itself, `gpython` for
AGENTS.md:336:the backend type, and `dg` for shared point-value materialization). It owns:
AGENTS.md:337:- shape properties (`num_dims`/`num_comps`/`num_cells`/`bounds`), `grid`/`values`,
AGENTS.md:338:- `backend` (`"gkyl"`/`"numpy"`) and `native` (the raw `GkylArray` for the kernels),
AGENTS.md:339:- `push`, `clone` (backend-aware deep copy via `type(self)`), and **`_result(...)`** —
AGENTS.md:340:  the one "mutate-self vs. emit-new" decision point every verb funnels through,
AGENTS.md:341:- pure state readers only: `__array__` (refuses on gkyl-backed data),
AGENTS.md:342:  `__repr__`/`__str__`, `info`, `is_interpolated`.
AGENTS.md:343:`gdatastate/collection.py` has `flatten_datasets` (shared by the multi-dataset entry points).
AGENTS.md:344:`gdatastate/guards.py` centralizes the field-domain check (`backend == "gkyl"` → raise with
AGENTS.md:345:the standard ".interpolate() first" message) that several `operations`/`diagnostics` verbs
AGENTS.md:346:need but that isn't itself a verb, so it lives here rather than in `operations`.
AGENTS.md:347:`gdatastate/materialize.py` owns the shared conversion from native nodal/quad values to
AGENTS.md:348:a NumPy-backed state used by every terminal consumer.
AGENTS.md:349:
AGENTS.md:350:### `api/` — the fluent surface (`api/gdata.py`, `api/load.py`)
AGENTS.md:351:`class GData(GDataState)` adds the **fluent verb methods** (`.interpolate()`, `.select()`,
AGENTS.md:352:`.plot()`, `.save()`, `.info` inherited) and the **computing operators**
AGENTS.md:353:(`+ - * / **`, reflected, `__neg__`/`__abs__`, `__array_ufunc__`). Because it lives
AGENTS.md:354:*above* `operations`, exact verbs are static class-body aliases to their canonical
AGENTS.md:355:operation — no wrapper, runtime `setattr`, or lazy import. `pg.load(...)`
AGENTS.md:356:returns a `GData`.
AGENTS.md:357:
AGENTS.md:358:`gdata/gdatagroup.py` mirrors the same move one level up: `class GDataGroup(gdatastate.GDataStateGroup)`
AGENTS.md:359:adds broadcasting — any attribute not defined on the class is resolved by `__getattr__`,
AGENTS.md:360:looked up on every member, so a verb call broadcasts across the whole group without a
AGENTS.md:361:single verb body being duplicated. `gdata/verbs.py` holds the handful of verbs that
AGENTS.md:362:combine *several* datasets and so have no single `self` to hang off of a class —
AGENTS.md:363:`collect`, `evaluate`, `relchange`, `animate` — each a direct alias to the matching
AGENTS.md:364:`operations` function; `GData` and `GDataGroup` both call through these same
AGENTS.md:365:module-level functions for their own methods, so the functional and fluent spellings
AGENTS.md:366:of a multi-dataset verb can never drift apart.
AGENTS.md:367:
AGENTS.md:368:**The trick that removes the cycle:** `operations` verbs are typed on `GDataState` but *return*
AGENTS.md:369:the caller's concrete class, because `_result` builds `type(self)()`. So `operations` never needs
AGENTS.md:370:to import `gdata`, yet the whole fluent chain stays `GData`. See `HIERARCHY_2.md`.
AGENTS.md:371:
AGENTS.md:372:### `operations/` — the data-transformation library (the single seam)
AGENTS.md:373:Flat core verbs have one module each and domain transformations live in named
AGENTS.md:374:subpackages exposed from `operations/__init__.py`. Contract:
AGENTS.md:375:`op(data: GDataState, *, ..., inplace=False, tag=None, label=None) -> GDataState`.
AGENTS.md:376:Flat modules hold equation-blind core verbs. Domain subpackages may know the
AGENTS.md:377:geometry or representation of one equation system while still only
AGENTS.md:378:transforming/re-expressing data; `operations/gyrokinetics/` owns the R-Z and
AGENTS.md:379:flux-surface projections. Code that interprets components to derive a new
AGENTS.md:380:physical conclusion belongs in `diagnostics/`.
AGENTS.md:381:Implemented: `interpolate` (the bridge verb: gkyl-backed in, numpy-backed out),
AGENTS.md:382:`select` (field-domain only), `info`, `integrate`
AGENTS.md:383:(terminal; runs inside Gkeyll on modal data), `represent`/`apply` (the explicit
AGENTS.md:384:value_form verbs behind `.to_modal()/.to_nodal()/.to_quad()/.apply()`),
AGENTS.md:385:`arithmetic` (`binary` + `apply_ufunc`), which **dispatches on `backend`**: modal
AGENTS.md:386:operands → `dg.modal` kernel calls; numpy operands → the NumPy path; mixed
AGENTS.md:387:domains or mixed value_forms → error, plus the field-domain analysis verbs
AGENTS.md:388:(`fft`, `magsq`, `relchange`, `mask`, `collect`, `grid`, `val2coord`,
AGENTS.md:389:`extract_input`, `fit` (its `window=True` mode covers growth-rate-style
AGENTS.md:390:leading-window fits), `differentiate`, `evaluate`, `map`); and the modal-native
AGENTS.md:391:verbs `average` (weighted average over a dimension subset via Gkeyll's
AGENTS.md:392:`gkyl_array_average`) and `eval_at_coord_proj` (eval at physical coordinates,
AGENTS.md:393:projected onto the lower-dimensional basis for the surviving directions) —
AGENTS.md:394:both terminal-adjacent like `represent`: they emit a new, lower-dimensional
AGENTS.md:395:dataset that stays modal/gkyl-native, so it composes with further
AGENTS.md:396:`.to_nodal()`/`.interpolate()`/`.average()`/`.eval_at_coord_proj()` calls
AGENTS.md:397:rather than dropping to NumPy. `local_poly` bridges modal coefficients to a
AGENTS.md:398:discontinuity-preserving plotting mesh.
AGENTS.md:399:`operations.plot`/`animate`/`plotly`/`plotly_animate`/`pyvista` are direct
AGENTS.md:400:aliases of their canonical `render` callables.
AGENTS.md:401:All terminal consumers share `gdatastate.materialize_point_values`, so the
AGENTS.md:402:point-value capability rule has one home. Verbs wrap the layers below; they
AGENTS.md:403:don't reimplement.
AGENTS.md:404:
AGENTS.md:405:### `diagnostics/` — equation-specific physics (COMPOSITION, above `gdata`)
AGENTS.md:406:The layer that knows what the numbers *mean* — and the ONLY package in the
AGENTS.md:407:COMPOSITION tier. Its four packages mirror Gkeyll's model-family folders:
AGENTS.md:408:
AGENTS.md:409:- `moments/` owns `five_moment`, `ten_moment`, `mhd`, `plasma` (plasma
AGENTS.md:410:  parameters), `multispecies` (`energetics`, `accumulate_current`), `rotations`
AGENTS.md:411:  (par/perp to B), and the five-moment `enstrophy`/`ke_dke` frame programs.
AGENTS.md:412:- `vlasov/` owns distribution-function frame transforms (`kinetic`) and
AGENTS.md:413:  particle trajectories (`trajectory`).
AGENTS.md:414:- `pkpm/` owns Laguerre reconstruction and `load_pkpm`.
AGENTS.md:415:- `gyrokinetics/` owns distf/quantity loaders, the quantity registry (Tpar,
AGENTS.md:416:  beta, drift velocities), and `energy_balance`/`particle_balance`/`nodes`.
AGENTS.md:417:
AGENTS.md:418:R-Z mapping and theta-phi flux-surface
AGENTS.md:419:extraction are gyrokinetic operations; their old diagnostic module paths are
AGENTS.md:420:compatibility aliases for the current major version. Contract: a diagnostic takes loaded
AGENTS.md:421:data — one or several `GData` — plus physical scalars as keyword-only
AGENTS.md:422:options, and returns `GDataState` (via `_result`, same inplace/tag/label
AGENTS.md:423:contract as a verb) or a Figure; it is built entirely from the public
AGENTS.md:424:vocabulary below it (`operations`, `gdatastate`, `numerics`, `gdata`) and nothing below the
AGENTS.md:425:surfaces imports it. The `render` edge is pre-authorized for this layer (a
AGENTS.md:426:program diagnostic may want `render.plot()`'s generic panel layout), but as
AGENTS.md:427:of this writing every program module builds its own bespoke figure directly
AGENTS.md:428:with `matplotlib` instead.
AGENTS.md:429:
AGENTS.md:430:**Each equation model owns its loading internally** — there is no `loaders/`
AGENTS.md:431:package. Entry points like `gyrokinetics.load_gk_quantity(...)` (naming-
AGENTS.md:432:convention load + registry dispatch, "physics-ready data by name") and
AGENTS.md:433:`pkpm.load_pkpm(...)` live beside the physics they feed, because a quantity's
AGENTS.md:434:ingredient files and its formula are one piece of equation knowledge. The
AGENTS.md:435:only shared piece is `diagnostics/discovery.py` — equation-blind
AGENTS.md:436:output-stem/frame discovery, the one home for Gkeyll's file-naming
AGENTS.md:437:convention; equation loaders and programs resolve files through it, never
AGENTS.md:438:with private globbing.
AGENTS.md:439:
AGENTS.md:440:Functions have real names (`moments.five_moment.pressure(d, gas_gamma=…)`), never
AGENTS.md:441:string dispatch; each equation module's `VARIABLES` table maps the CLI's
AGENTS.md:442:quantity-name vocabulary (`"density"`, `"pressure"`, …) to those functions —
AGENTS.md:443:the one home for that vocabulary. These are **free functions, not `GData`
AGENTS.md:444:methods**: the layer sits above the fluent surface. (This layer absorbed the
AGENTS.md:445:former `models/` package — array physics now lives as private helpers inside
AGENTS.md:446:the equation module that uses it.)
AGENTS.md:447:
AGENTS.md:448:### Engine layers — `dg/`, `io/` (may import `gpython` only)
AGENTS.md:449:- **`dg/`** — Gkeyll-kernel orchestration. `dg/interpolate.py` is the one-way modal→NumPy
AGENTS.md:450:  bridge (matrix from `gpython.basis`, applied per cell with `tensordot`; nodal-basis
AGENTS.md:451:  files convert through the exact `nodal_to_modal` matrix first); `dg/modal.py`
AGENTS.md:452:  holds the operations that stay modal (weak algebra, `lincomb`, `shift_mean`,
AGENTS.md:453:  `power`, `integrate`); `dg/rep.py` holds the explicit value_form changes
AGENTS.md:454:  (modal·nodal·quad) and `apply_pointwise` — all on native arrays.
AGENTS.md:455:- **`io/`** — file I/O: `read()` dispatches over a reader registry. `GkylCReader`
AGENTS.md:456:  (first) reads field files entirely inside Gkeyll (`gkyl_grid_array_new_from_file`)
AGENTS.md:457:  and returns a native `GkylArray`; the pure-Python `GkylReader` is the fallback for
AGENTS.md:458:  no-library installs, partial loads, and dynvectors. `save()` supports
AGENTS.md:459:  `gkyl`/`txt`/`npy`/`vtk`. Readers fill a plain `ctx` dict and return
AGENTS.md:460:  `(grid, values)` — they never import `gdatastate`.
AGENTS.md:461:
AGENTS.md:462:### Leaves — `numerics/` (imports nothing), `gpython/` (the foreign floor)
AGENTS.md:463:- **`numerics/`** — pure NumPy: `idx_parser` (selection strings) and `elementwise`
AGENTS.md:464:  (`grids_compatible`). No `GData`, ever.
AGENTS.md:465:- **`gpython/`** — **the only doorway to the foreign world** (a test enforces this),
AGENTS.md:466:  and it is a *compiled* one (GKEYLL_C_SHIM.md): the gpython shim
AGENTS.md:467:  (`gkeyll/core/zero/{gkyl_gpython.h, gpython.c}`) lives **in the gkeyll tree** and is
AGENTS.md:468:  compiled by Gkeyll's own `make core` *into* `libg0core.so` — it holds every
AGENTS.md:469:  struct access, the by-value `struct gkyl_basis` convention, and the basis
AGENTS.md:470:  function-pointer dispatch, all checked by the C compiler against the headers
AGENTS.md:471:  in the same tree (shim and library can never drift apart).
AGENTS.md:472:  `csrc/_gpythonmodule.c` wraps `gkyl_gpython.h` (opaque handles + scalars + buffers
AGENTS.md:473:  only) into the `_gpython` extension, built by `scripts/build_gpython.sh` against
AGENTS.md:474:  the cloned `gkeyll/`'s `libg0core.so` (linked + rpath-bound, not dlopened).
AGENTS.md:475:  `_lib.py` imports the extension and performs the `GPYTHON_API_VERSION`
AGENTS.md:476:  handshake. `array.py`'s
AGENTS.md:477:  `GkylArray` holds the owning capsule (its destructor releases the C array;
AGENTS.md:478:  zero-copy constructions pin their NumPy buffer in the capsule, and `view()`
AGENTS.md:479:  ties the ndarray's `base` chain to the capsule so views outlive their dataset
AGENTS.md:480:  — never hand out C memory without that pin). `basis.py` builds every matrix
AGENTS.md:481:  by evaluating Gkeyll's own basis through the shim: `eval_matrix(points)`,
AGENTS.md:482:  nodal↔modal, modal↔quad (+ Gauss rules). No struct layout, signature, or
AGENTS.md:483:  ctypes declaration exists in Python. `gpython.available()` is the single
AGENTS.md:484:  capability switch.
AGENTS.md:485:
AGENTS.md:486:### `render/` — visualization backend (`render/matplotlib.py`)
AGENTS.md:487:`plot(*datasets, ...)` is the one canonical plotting function: 1-D lines / 2-D
AGENTS.md:488:pcolormesh, one panel per component, multi-dataset overlay/grouping, saving,
AGENTS.md:489:display, and every public plot option. The facade, fluent method, operations
AGENTS.md:490:namespace, and generated CLI all point to this same callable.
AGENTS.md:491:
AGENTS.md:492:### `__init__.py` — the facade (pure re-export)
AGENTS.md:493:Gathers the public names from the layer that owns each: `load`/`GData` ← `gdata`,
AGENTS.md:494:`plot` ← `render`, `info` ← `operations`, `save` ← `io`, `load_gk_quantity`/
AGENTS.md:495:`load_gk_distf`/`available_gk_quantities` ← `diagnostics.gyrokinetics`. **It
AGENTS.md:496:contains no function or class definitions** (a test enforces this).
AGENTS.md:497:
AGENTS.md:498:`_version.py` sits beside `__init__.py` (same `""` layer) and supplies
AGENTS.md:499:`version_report` — `pgkyl --version`'s debugging-statistics report, not a
AGENTS.md:500:computing verb, but re-exported through the facade like everything else here
AGENTS.md:501:(so `cli/app.py` stays a pure facade consumer). It reads `gpython.available()`/
AGENTS.md:502:`gpython.build_info()` (hence `""`'s extra allowed edge, `-> gpython`), git
AGENTS.md:503:(the postgkyl commit this checkout is at) and `importlib.metadata` (key
AGENTS.md:504:dependency versions). `version_report(version)` takes the version string as
AGENTS.md:505:a parameter rather than importing `postgkyl.__version__` itself, so
AGENTS.md:506:`__init__.py`'s own `from postgkyl._version import version_report` line has
AGENTS.md:507:no ordering dependency on the `__version__` assignment below it.
AGENTS.md:508:
AGENTS.md:509:### `cli/` — the CLI (chained pipeline on pure Click)
AGENTS.md:510:`cli/app.py` defines `PgkylGroup(click.Group)` with `chain=True`; the chaining loop and
AGENTS.md:511:callback-before-dispatch are **native to Click**. At import time it discovers the
AGENTS.md:512:public script API, compiles its `CommandSpec` records, and lowers every record through
AGENTS.md:513:the one generic compiler. There is no `cli/commands/` package and no hand-authored
AGENTS.md:514:subcommand. Python underscores are mechanically rendered as CLI dashes in command and
AGENTS.md:515:option names (`local_poly` → `local-poly`, `num_moms` → `--num-moms`). The custom
AGENTS.md:516:compiler also adds a one-letter option (`--num-moms` → `-n`) when that initial is
AGENTS.md:517:unique within the command; conflicting initials receive no short option and `-h` is
AGENTS.md:518:reserved for help. The custom group code handles spelling-only aliases/unambiguous
AGENTS.md:519:abbreviations and expands a bare
AGENTS.md:520:filename to `load --file-name`; aliases never change a generated command's parameters
AGENTS.md:521:or execution. `format_commands` groups `pgkyl --help` under Verbs / Diagnostics /
AGENTS.md:522:Render / Utility; presentation does not change the flat, chainable inventory.
AGENTS.md:523:`--version` is a custom eager `click.option` (not `click.version_option`, since
AGENTS.md:524:the output is more than one string): its callback calls the facade's
AGENTS.md:525:`version_report(__version__)` (both imported via `from postgkyl import
AGENTS.md:526:__version__, version_report`, same as any other facade name) to print the
AGENTS.md:527:postgkyl commit,
AGENTS.md:528:the vendored Gkeyll commit/branch/build-date this build was linked against
AGENTS.md:529:(`gpython.build_info()`, generated by `scripts/build_gpython.sh` since
AGENTS.md:530:`gkeyll/` is a build-time-only clone — absent, it reports "not built"),
AGENTS.md:531:gpython-bridge availability, and interpreter/platform/dependency versions.
AGENTS.md:532:`--help` is wired through Click's own group help. The console entry point
AGENTS.md:533:object is `postgkyl.cli.app:cli`.
AGENTS.md:534:
AGENTS.md:535:`load` (or its bare-filename shorthand) exposes the script parameters
AGENTS.md:536:`--basis-type`, `--poly-order`, and `--value-form` — `basis_type`/`poly_order`/
AGENTS.md:537:`value_form` are properties of the data fixed once here at load time, so no
AGENTS.md:538:other verb command (`interpolate`, `local-poly`, …) repeats them.

examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:1:"""Gyrokinetic diagnostics: named quantities and distribution functions.
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:2:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:3:``postgkyl.diagnostics.gyrokinetics`` is another equation-specific module in
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:4:the diagnostics layer (like ``five_moment`` in
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:5:``examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py``), but for gyrokinetic
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:6:simulations it owns its own *loading* too -- a simulation's files follow a
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:7:naming convention (``<name>-<species>_<quantity>_<frame>.gkyl``), so instead
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:8:of calling ``pg.load`` on individual filenames, you ask for a quantity by
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:9:name and the loader resolves which files it needs:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:10:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:11:* ``pg.available_gk_quantities()`` lists the registered quantity names.
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:12:* ``pg.load_gk_quantity(quantity, species, name, frame, path=...)`` resolves
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:13:  the source file(s) for that quantity, computes it, and returns one
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:14:  ``GData`` per requested species -- already interpolated, ready to
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:15:  ``.select()``/``.plot()`` like anything else.
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:16:* ``pg.load_gk_distf(name=..., species=..., frame=..., ...)`` reconstructs a
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:17:  full distribution function from the saved ``Jf``-times-Jacobian(s) files
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:18:  (what the CLI's ``gk_distf`` command wraps).
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:19:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:20:This uses the ``rt_gk_tcv_iwl*`` fixtures staged in ``tests/test_data`` --
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:21:two related simulations: ``rt_gk_tcv_iwl_adapt_source_1x2v_p1`` wrote ion
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:22:Hamiltonian moments (``M0``/``M1`` are derivable from those), and
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:23:``rt_gk_tcv_iwl_1x2v_p1`` wrote the electron distribution function plus its
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:24:geometry (``geo_int_jacobtot_inv``).
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:25:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:26:Run directly:
examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py:27:    MPLBACKEND=Agg PYTHONPATH=src python examples/scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py

examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:1:"""The diagnostics layer: equation-specific physics on top of the same
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:2:``GData`` you get from ``pg.load``.
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:3:
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:4:``diagnostics`` sits *above* the fluent API (``operations``/``api``) and is
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:5:equation-blind-free by design: ``postgkyl.diagnostics.moments.five_moment`` knows the
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:6:Euler fluid moment layout (``[rho, rho*vx, rho*vy, rho*vz, E]``) and turns raw
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:7:conserved moments into primitive variables (density, velocity, pressure,
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:8:Mach number, ...). Diagnostics are **free functions**, not ``GData`` methods
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:9:-- ``fm.density(d)``, never ``d.density()`` -- because a diagnostic knows
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:10:about one specific equation system and a ``GData`` doesn't.
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:11:
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:12:This script builds a small 1D Sod shock-tube initial condition by hand (no
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:13:file needed -- any interpolated/NumPy-backed ``GData`` will do, whether it
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:14:came from ``pg.load(...).interpolate()`` or, as here, straight from
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:15:``.push()``) and reads off density, pressure, and Mach number.
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:16:
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:17:Run directly:
examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:18:    MPLBACKEND=Agg PYTHONPATH=src python examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py

examples/scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py:37:# A Sod shock tube: high density/pressure on the left, low on the right, at

tests/test_gpython_lib.py:89:
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:90:  `from package import submodule` tries `getattr(package, submodule)`
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:91:  BEFORE consulting `sys.modules`, and the real `postgkyl.gpython` package
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:92:  object already carries a `_gpython` attribute (set as a side effect of the
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:93:  real import at process start) -- so patching `sys.modules` alone is not
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:94:  enough. Both are patched here and restored unconditionally.
tests/test_gpython_lib.py:95:  """

tests/test_gpython_lib.py:106:    if self._had_attr:

examples/cli_tutorial.md:1:# `pgkyl` CLI tutorial
examples/cli_tutorial.md:2:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:3:Every command below is real: it runs against fixture files under
examples/cli_tutorial.md:4:`tests/test_data/` -- most committed directly, a few under
examples/cli_tutorial.md:5:`tests/test_data/generated/` and synthesized by `tests/generate_test_data.py`
examples/cli_tutorial.md:6:(run once, or on the first `pytest` invocation, which does it automatically)
examples/cli_tutorial.md:7:-- and `tests/test_examples.py` replays each one (via `click.testing.CliRunner`,
examples/cli_tutorial.md:8:from the repository root) as a regression check. If the CLI's surface ever
examples/cli_tutorial.md:9:changes in a way that breaks one of these commands, that test fails -- this
examples/cli_tutorial.md:10:file cannot silently drift out of date the way a hand-maintained tutorial can.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:11:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:12:Run any line yourself from the repository root, after `pip install -e .[test]`
examples/cli_tutorial.md:13:and (for the `tests/test_data/generated/` fixtures) `python
examples/cli_tutorial.md:14:tests/generate_test_data.py`.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:15:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:16:## 1. Inspect a file
examples/cli_tutorial.md:17:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:18:`info` is the "what is this?" command -- dimensions, components, grid,
examples/cli_tutorial.md:19:value range, and the DG basis/order it was written with.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:20:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:21:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:22:pgkyl tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_iwl_adapt_source_1x2v_p1-ion_HamiltonianMoments_250.gkyl info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:23:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:24:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:25:## 2. The chain: interpolate -> select -> plot
examples/cli_tutorial.md:26:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:27:Raw `.gkyl` files hold DG *coefficients*; `interpolate` bridges them onto a
examples/cli_tutorial.md:28:uniform mesh of plain values, `select` narrows down to one component (or one
examples/cli_tutorial.md:29:coordinate slice), and `plot` renders it. The CLI options are the Python
examples/cli_tutorial.md:30:parameters with dashes: `--show False` runs headless and `--saveas` writes a
examples/cli_tutorial.md:31:PNG.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:32:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:33:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:34:pgkyl tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_iwl_adapt_source_1x2v_p1-ion_HamiltonianMoments_250.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:35:    interpolate select --comp 0 plot --show False --saveas out.png
examples/cli_tutorial.md:36:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:37:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:38:Any unambiguous command-name prefix is accepted as a spelling-only alias
examples/cli_tutorial.md:39:(`interp` -> `interpolate`, `sel` -> `select`):
examples/cli_tutorial.md:40:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:41:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:42:pgkyl tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_iwl_adapt_source_1x2v_p1-ion_HamiltonianMoments_250.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:43:    interp sel --comp 0 info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:44:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:45:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:46:## 3. Discontinuity-preserving plots with `local-poly`
examples/cli_tutorial.md:47:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:48:`interpolate` produces a continuous refined mesh; `local-poly` instead
examples/cli_tutorial.md:49:evaluates the DG polynomial cell-by-cell and splices a NaN at every
examples/cli_tutorial.md:50:inter-cell interface, so a plot shows genuine discontinuities instead of
examples/cli_tutorial.md:51:smoothing over them -- useful for shocks or anything with jumps at cell
examples/cli_tutorial.md:52:boundaries.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:53:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:54:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:55:pgkyl tests/test_data/generated/distf_p2_0.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:56:    local-poly select --z1 0.0 --z2 0.0 plot --show False --saveas out.png
examples/cli_tutorial.md:57:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:58:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:59:## 4. DynVector inspection and `fit`
examples/cli_tutorial.md:60:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:61:`.gkyl` files without a spatial grid (diagnostics like a field-energy history)
examples/cli_tutorial.md:62:are DynVectors: `info` summarizes the data, and `fit` fits a model to it (here,
examples/cli_tutorial.md:63:a straight line to the series vs. time -- the growth-rate use case).
examples/cli_tutorial.md:64:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:65:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:66:pgkyl tests/test_data/generated/energy_dynvec.gkyl info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:67:pgkyl tests/test_data/generated/energy_dynvec.gkyl fit --fit-type linear
examples/cli_tutorial.md:68:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:69:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:70:## 5. Combining datasets: `evaluate`
examples/cli_tutorial.md:71:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:72:`evaluate` runs a Reverse Polish Notation expression over every dataset
examples/cli_tutorial.md:73:currently loaded: `fN` refers to the `N`-th one in load order (`f` alone
examples/cli_tutorial.md:74:means `f0`), so `"f0 f1 -"` subtracts the second dataset from the first --
examples/cli_tutorial.md:75:e.g. two frames of the same field, to see how it changed between them.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:76:(`fN[c]` selects component `c` of dataset `N`; don't confuse that with
examples/cli_tutorial.md:77:indexing datasets themselves -- there is no `f[N]` form.) Data must be
examples/cli_tutorial.md:78:`interpolate`d first, same as `select`/`plot`.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:79:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:80:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:81:pgkyl tests/test_data/generated/distf_p2_0.gkyl tests/test_data/generated/distf_p2_1.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:82:    interpolate evaluate "f0 f1 -" info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:83:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:84:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:85:## 6. Gyrokinetics: pre-named quantities and distribution functions
examples/cli_tutorial.md:86:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:87:`gyrokinetics-load-gk-quantity` loads one of a registry of named gyrokinetic
examples/cli_tutorial.md:88:quantities (listed in its generated `--quantity` choices) straight from a simulation's naming convention --
examples/cli_tutorial.md:89:no manual file paths. `--name` is the simulation's *name prefix* (not a path);
examples/cli_tutorial.md:90:`--path` is the directory to look in.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:91:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:92:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:93:pgkyl gyrokinetics-load-gk-quantity --help
examples/cli_tutorial.md:94:pgkyl gyrokinetics-load-gk-quantity --quantity geo_int_jacobtot_inv --species "" \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:95:    --name rt_gk_tcv_iwl_1x2v_p1 --path tests/test_data info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:96:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:97:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:98:`gyrokinetics-load-gk-distf` reconstructs a full distribution function from the saved
examples/cli_tutorial.md:99:`Jf`-times-Jacobian(s) files (here `--name` *does* include the directory, since
examples/cli_tutorial.md:100:the simulation name itself includes the directory):
examples/cli_tutorial.md:101:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:102:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:103:pgkyl gyrokinetics-load-gk-distf --name tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_iwl_1x2v_p1 \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:104:    --species elc --frame 250 \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:105:    --jacobtot-inv-file tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_iwl_1x2v_p1-geo_int_jacobtot_inv.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:106:    info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:107:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:108:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:109:## 7. Map a gyrokinetic field to R-Z
examples/cli_tutorial.md:110:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:111:`gk-rz` is a data transformation: it interpolates one raw DG component and
examples/cli_tutorial.md:112:maps it onto the physical poloidal plane. Geometry is inferred from the
examples/cli_tutorial.md:113:field's filename, preferring nodal geometry and falling back to modal
examples/cli_tutorial.md:114:`mapc2p` geometry. The CLI and Python calls below use the same operation and
examples/cli_tutorial.md:115:defaults:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:116:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:117:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:118:pgkyl tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_nt_iwl_3x2v_p1-elc_M0_5.gkyl \
examples/cli_tutorial.md:119:    gk-rz --nz-interp 2 info
examples/cli_tutorial.md:120:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:121:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:122:```python
examples/cli_tutorial.md:123:import postgkyl as pg
examples/cli_tutorial.md:124:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:125:mapped = pg.load(
examples/cli_tutorial.md:126:    "tests/test_data/rt_gk_tcv_nt_iwl_3x2v_p1-elc_M0_5.gkyl"
examples/cli_tutorial.md:127:).gk_rz(nz_interp=2)
examples/cli_tutorial.md:128:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:129:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:130:## 8. Saving to another format
examples/cli_tutorial.md:131:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:132:`save` writes the current dataset(s) out as `gkyl`/`txt`/`npy`/`vtk`.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:133:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:134:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:135:pgkyl tests/test_data/generated/distf_p2_0.gkyl save --out-name distf --extension npy
examples/cli_tutorial.md:136:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:137:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:138:## 9. One API-derived command inventory
examples/cli_tutorial.md:139:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:140:Every loaded file becomes a dataset in the current chain. The command list is
examples/cli_tutorial.md:141:compiled from the script API, so `--help` is the authoritative inventory and
examples/cli_tutorial.md:142:every Python underscore appears as a CLI dash.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:143:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:144:```bash
examples/cli_tutorial.md:145:pgkyl --help
examples/cli_tutorial.md:146:```
examples/cli_tutorial.md:147:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:148:## See also
examples/cli_tutorial.md:149:
examples/cli_tutorial.md:150:- `pgkyl --help` lists every registered command, grouped by section
examples/cli_tutorial.md:151:  (Verbs / Diagnostics / Render / Utility).
examples/cli_tutorial.md:152:- `pgkyl <command> --help` documents that command's options -- most carry a
examples/cli_tutorial.md:153:  worked example in their docstring, e.g. `pgkyl local-poly --help`.
examples/cli_tutorial.md:154:- `examples/scripts/` is the Python-script equivalent of this tutorial (the
examples/cli_tutorial.md:155:  fluent `GData` API instead of the chained CLI).

tests/test_dg_map.py:31:def _project_1d(fn, lower, upper, cells, basis_type, poly_order):
tests/test_dg_map.py:32:  """Exact per-cell modal coefficients of ``fn(z)`` for a 1-D basis.
tests/test_dg_map.py:33:
tests/test_dg_map.py:34:  ``fn`` must be exactly representable in the basis on every cell (e.g. any
tests/test_dg_map.py:35:  polynomial of degree <= poly_order) -- projecting through the node points
tests/test_dg_map.py:36:  and back through the exact nodal<->modal change of basis reproduces it
tests/test_dg_map.py:37:  exactly, independent of the mapping code under test.
tests/test_dg_map.py:38:  """
tests/test_dg_map.py:39:  nb = gpython.basis.num_basis(basis_type, 1, poly_order)
tests/test_dg_map.py:40:  node_eta = gpython.basis.node_coords(basis_type, 1, poly_order)[:, 0]
tests/test_dg_map.py:41:  n2m = gpython.basis.nodal_to_modal_matrix(basis_type, 1, poly_order)
tests/test_dg_map.py:42:  dz = (upper - lower) / cells
tests/test_dg_map.py:43:  centers = lower + (np.arange(cells) + 0.5) * dz
tests/test_dg_map.py:44:  nodal_z = centers[:, None] + 0.5 * dz * node_eta[None, :]  # (cells, nb)
tests/test_dg_map.py:45:  nodal_vals = fn(nodal_z)
tests/test_dg_map.py:46:  return nodal_vals @ n2m.T, nodal_vals  # (modal, nodal) both (cells, nb)

examples/README.md:1:# Postgkyl examples
examples/README.md:2:
examples/README.md:3:Two parallel tutorials over the same golden path -- `load -> interpolate ->
examples/README.md:4:select -> plot` -- one per interface:
examples/README.md:5:
examples/README.md:6:- **`scripts/`** -- the fluent Python API (`import postgkyl as pg`).
examples/README.md:7:- **`cli_tutorial.md`** -- the equivalent `pgkyl` command-line chains.
examples/README.md:8:
examples/README.md:9:Both are executable, and both are tested: `tests/test_examples.py` runs
examples/README.md:10:every script and replays every command quoted in the markdown tutorial, so
examples/README.md:11:an example that stops working (an API rename, a removed option) fails the
examples/README.md:12:test suite instead of quietly rotting. Treat that file as the single source
examples/README.md:13:of truth for "does the tutorial still work," not just this README.
examples/README.md:14:
examples/README.md:15:## Scripts
examples/README.md:16:
examples/README.md:17:| Script | What it covers |
examples/README.md:18:| --- | --- |
examples/README.md:19:| [`01_quickstart.py`](scripts/01_quickstart.py) | `pg.load` → `.interpolate()` → `.select()` → `.plot()` → `.save()`/reload |
examples/README.md:20:| [`02_arithmetic_and_numpy.py`](scripts/02_arithmetic_and_numpy.py) | Weak DG algebra on raw modal data (`*`, `/`, `+`, `.integrate()`) vs. plain NumPy math after `.interpolate()`, and the guardrail between them |
examples/README.md:21:| [`03_diagnostics_five_moment.py`](scripts/03_diagnostics_five_moment.py) | The `diagnostics` layer: equation-specific physics (`postgkyl.diagnostics.moments.five_moment`) on top of a `GData`, on a hand-built Sod shock tube |
examples/README.md:22:| [`04_gyrokinetics.py`](scripts/04_gyrokinetics.py) | The gyrokinetic diagnostics: `pg.load_gk_quantity` (named moments/geometry, resolved by naming convention) and `pg.load_gk_distf` (full distribution function), on the `rt_gk_tcv_iwl*` fixtures |
examples/README.md:23:| [`05_gk_rz.py`](scripts/05_gk_rz.py) | The gyrokinetic R-Z operation: one-line fluent and functional calls plus projection reuse over multiple toroidal angles |
examples/README.md:24:| [`mirror_comparison.py`](scripts/mirror_comparison.py) | A four-panel algorithm-sensitivity figure from two analytic, symmetric 1-D p1 modal-serendipity datasets, with joined linear/log axes |
examples/README.md:25:
examples/README.md:26:Run one directly:
examples/README.md:27:
examples/README.md:28:```bash
examples/README.md:29:pip install -e .[test]
examples/README.md:30:MPLBACKEND=Agg PYTHONPATH=src python examples/scripts/01_quickstart.py
examples/README.md:31:```
examples/README.md:32:
examples/README.md:33:Each script prints what it's doing as it goes and asserts the invariants it
examples/README.md:34:demonstrates, so a successful run ending in `... OK` is itself a (manual)
examples/README.md:35:confirmation that the example still holds. Output files (PNGs, a `.gkyl`
examples/README.md:36:round trip) land in `examples/scripts/output/` by default, or wherever
examples/README.md:37:`PGKYL_EXAMPLE_OUTPUT` points if that environment variable is set (this is
examples/README.md:38:how `tests/test_examples.py` redirects them into a temp directory instead of
examples/README.md:39:the repo).
examples/README.md:40:
examples/README.md:41:## CLI
examples/README.md:42:
examples/README.md:43:See [`cli_tutorial.md`](cli_tutorial.md) -- inspecting a file, the
examples/README.md:44:`interpolate`/`select`/`plot` chain, discontinuity-preserving plots with
examples/README.md:45:`local-poly`, DynVector `info`/`fit`, the gyrokinetic loaders
examples/README.md:46:(`gyrokinetics-load-gk-quantity`, `gyrokinetics-load-gk-distf`), the `gk-rz`
examples/README.md:47:transformation, `save`, and the generated command inventory.
examples/README.md:48:
examples/README.md:49:## Running the tests
examples/README.md:50:
examples/README.md:51:```bash
examples/README.md:52:pytest tests/test_examples.py -v
examples/README.md:53:```
examples/README.md:54:
examples/README.md:55:Both halves need a compiled Gkeyll (`libg0core.so`) to run -- every fixture
examples/README.md:56:here is a native `.gkyl` file, so the tests are skipped (not failed)
examples/README.md:57:when `postgkyl.gpython.available()` is `False`, matching the rest of the
examples/README.md:58:test suite's `needs_gkeyll` convention.

tests/generate_test_data.py:135:def _c2p_stretch_values(
tests/generate_test_data.py:136:    cells: list[int],
tests/generate_test_data.py:137:    phys_lo: list[float],
tests/generate_test_data.py:138:    phys_hi: list[float],
tests/generate_test_data.py:139:    num_modes: int,
tests/generate_test_data.py:140:) -> np.ndarray:
tests/generate_test_data.py:141:    """Modal DG coefficients for a linear stretch mapping (comp [0,1]^n → phys).
tests/generate_test_data.py:142:
tests/generate_test_data.py:143:    For each cell the mapping is:
tests/generate_test_data.py:144:        coord_d(xi') = coord_mid_d + (dx_phys_d/2) * xi'_d
tests/generate_test_data.py:145:    Modal serendipity coefficients (any poly_order):
tests/generate_test_data.py:146:        c_0 = 2 * coord_mid       (constant mode, normalized by 1/2)
tests/generate_test_data.py:147:        c_{d+1} = dx_phys / sqrt(3) (linear mode in direction d)
tests/generate_test_data.py:148:        all higher modes = 0      (linear function has no quadratic terms)
tests/generate_test_data.py:149:    """
tests/generate_test_data.py:150:    ndim = len(cells)
tests/generate_test_data.py:151:    dx = [(phys_hi[d] - phys_lo[d]) / cells[d] for d in range(ndim)]
tests/generate_test_data.py:152:    values = np.zeros((*cells, ndim * num_modes))
tests/generate_test_data.py:153:
tests/generate_test_data.py:154:    grids = np.meshgrid(*[np.arange(cells[d]) for d in range(ndim)], indexing="ij")
tests/generate_test_data.py:155:    for d in range(ndim):
tests/generate_test_data.py:156:        mid = phys_lo[d] + dx[d] * (grids[d] + 0.5)
tests/generate_test_data.py:157:        off = d * num_modes
tests/generate_test_data.py:158:        values[..., off] = 2.0 * mid              # constant mode
tests/generate_test_data.py:159:        values[..., off + 1 + d] = dx[d] / _SQRT3 # linear mode in d-th direction
tests/generate_test_data.py:160:    return values
tests/generate_test_data.py:161:
tests/generate_test_data.py:162:
tests/generate_test_data.py:163:def _c2p_rotation_values(
tests/generate_test_data.py:164:    cells: list[int],
tests/generate_test_data.py:165:    comp_lo: list[float],
tests/generate_test_data.py:166:    comp_hi: list[float],
tests/generate_test_data.py:167:    angle: float,
tests/generate_test_data.py:168:    num_modes: int,
tests/generate_test_data.py:169:) -> np.ndarray:
tests/generate_test_data.py:170:    """Modal DG coefficients for a 2D rotation mapping by *angle* radians.
tests/generate_test_data.py:171:
tests/generate_test_data.py:172:    The computational domain is [comp_lo[0], comp_hi[0]] x [comp_lo[1], comp_hi[1]].
tests/generate_test_data.py:173:    The mapping is x = xi*cos - eta*sin, y = xi*sin + eta*cos.
tests/generate_test_data.py:174:    Only valid for 2D serendipity; the linear rotation is exact at any poly_order.
tests/generate_test_data.py:175:    """
tests/generate_test_data.py:176:    assert len(cells) == 2, "rotation mapping only implemented for 2D"
tests/generate_test_data.py:177:    ca, sa = np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)
tests/generate_test_data.py:178:    N_x, N_y = cells
tests/generate_test_data.py:179:    dxi  = (comp_hi[0] - comp_lo[0]) / N_x
tests/generate_test_data.py:180:    deta = (comp_hi[1] - comp_lo[1]) / N_y
tests/generate_test_data.py:181:
tests/generate_test_data.py:182:    ii, jj = np.mgrid[0:N_x, 0:N_y]
tests/generate_test_data.py:183:    xi_mid  = comp_lo[0] + dxi  * (ii + 0.5)
tests/generate_test_data.py:184:    eta_mid = comp_lo[1] + deta * (jj + 0.5)
tests/generate_test_data.py:185:
tests/generate_test_data.py:186:    x_mid = xi_mid * ca - eta_mid * sa
tests/generate_test_data.py:187:    y_mid = xi_mid * sa + eta_mid * ca
tests/generate_test_data.py:188:
tests/generate_test_data.py:189:    values = np.zeros((N_x, N_y, 2 * num_modes))
tests/generate_test_data.py:190:    # x-coordinate modal coefficients
tests/generate_test_data.py:191:    values[..., 0] = 2.0 * x_mid              # constant
tests/generate_test_data.py:192:    values[..., 1] = dxi  * ca / _SQRT3       # xi'-mode (dx/dxi' * mapping factor)
tests/generate_test_data.py:193:    values[..., 2] = -deta * sa / _SQRT3      # eta'-mode
tests/generate_test_data.py:194:    # y-coordinate modal coefficients
tests/generate_test_data.py:195:    values[..., num_modes + 0] = 2.0 * y_mid
tests/generate_test_data.py:196:    values[..., num_modes + 1] = dxi  * sa / _SQRT3
tests/generate_test_data.py:197:    values[..., num_modes + 2] = deta * ca / _SQRT3
tests/generate_test_data.py:198:    return values

tests/generate_test_data.py:205:def _mirror_comparison_profiles(z: np.ndarray, alpha: float) -> np.ndarray:
tests/generate_test_data.py:206:    """Symmetric beam profiles used by the alpha-convergence example.
tests/generate_test_data.py:207:
tests/generate_test_data.py:208:    Density and both temperatures are even in ``z``; parallel velocity is
tests/generate_test_data.py:209:    odd.  ``alpha`` introduces a small, pedestal-localized difference so the
tests/generate_test_data.py:210:    two generated datasets remain close enough to read as a convergence
tests/generate_test_data.py:211:    comparison.  Components are already in the plotting units used by the
tests/generate_test_data.py:212:    example: m^-3, m/s, keV, and keV.
tests/generate_test_data.py:213:    """
tests/generate_test_data.py:214:    if alpha <= 0.0:
tests/generate_test_data.py:215:        raise ValueError("alpha must be positive")
tests/generate_test_data.py:216:
tests/generate_test_data.py:217:    radius = np.abs(z)
tests/generate_test_data.py:218:    sensitivity = np.log10(alpha / 2.0e-5)
tests/generate_test_data.py:219:    pedestal = np.exp(-((radius - 0.86) / 0.16) ** 2)
tests/generate_test_data.py:220:
tests/generate_test_data.py:221:    density = (
tests/generate_test_data.py:222:        1.01e13
tests/generate_test_data.py:223:        + 2.45e19 / (1.0 + np.exp((radius - 0.92) / 0.08))
tests/generate_test_data.py:224:        + 4.5e18 * np.exp(-(radius / 0.55) ** 4)
tests/generate_test_data.py:225:    )
tests/generate_test_data.py:226:    velocity = (
tests/generate_test_data.py:227:        1.30e6 * np.tanh(z / 0.05)
tests/generate_test_data.py:228:        / (1.0 + np.exp((0.82 - radius) / 0.05))
tests/generate_test_data.py:229:    )
tests/generate_test_data.py:230:    t_parallel = (
tests/generate_test_data.py:231:        0.101
tests/generate_test_data.py:232:        + 11.8 / (1.0 + np.exp((radius - 0.90) / 0.10))
tests/generate_test_data.py:233:        + 0.4 * np.exp(-((radius - 0.55) / 0.15) ** 2)
tests/generate_test_data.py:234:    )
tests/generate_test_data.py:235:    t_perpendicular = (
tests/generate_test_data.py:236:        0.101
tests/generate_test_data.py:237:        + 20.8 / (1.0 + np.exp((radius - 0.98) / 0.13))
tests/generate_test_data.py:238:        + 10.0 * np.exp(-((radius - 0.86) / 0.10) ** 2)
tests/generate_test_data.py:239:    )
tests/generate_test_data.py:240:
tests/generate_test_data.py:241:    return np.stack([
tests/generate_test_data.py:242:        density * (1.0 - 0.025 * sensitivity * pedestal),
tests/generate_test_data.py:243:        velocity * (1.0 + 0.020 * sensitivity * pedestal),
tests/generate_test_data.py:244:        t_parallel * (1.0 + 0.035 * sensitivity * pedestal),
tests/generate_test_data.py:245:        t_perpendicular * (1.0 + 0.030 * sensitivity * pedestal),
tests/generate_test_data.py:246:    ], axis=-1)

tests/generate_test_data.py:249:def _project_1d_p1(fn, lower: float, upper: float, cells: int, *args) -> np.ndarray:
tests/generate_test_data.py:250:    """Cellwise L2 projection of a vector-valued analytic function onto p1.
tests/generate_test_data.py:251:
tests/generate_test_data.py:252:    The 1-D modal serendipity basis is ``(1/sqrt(2), sqrt(3/2)*xi)`` on
tests/generate_test_data.py:253:    ``[-1, 1]``.  Eight-point Gauss quadrature resolves the smooth analytic
tests/generate_test_data.py:254:    profiles well within each cell.  The result is field-blocked as Gkeyll
tests/generate_test_data.py:255:    expects: ``[f0_mode0, f0_mode1, f1_mode0, ...]``.
tests/generate_test_data.py:256:    """
tests/generate_test_data.py:257:    xi, weights = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(8)
tests/generate_test_data.py:258:    dz = (upper - lower) / cells
tests/generate_test_data.py:259:    centers = lower + (np.arange(cells) + 0.5) * dz
tests/generate_test_data.py:260:    z = centers[:, None] + 0.5 * dz * xi[None, :]
tests/generate_test_data.py:261:    samples = fn(z, *args)
tests/generate_test_data.py:262:    basis = np.stack([
tests/generate_test_data.py:263:        np.full_like(xi, 1.0 / np.sqrt(2.0)),
tests/generate_test_data.py:264:        np.sqrt(3.0 / 2.0) * xi,
tests/generate_test_data.py:265:    ], axis=-1)
tests/generate_test_data.py:266:    coefficients = np.einsum("cqf,qb,q->cfb", samples, basis, weights)
tests/generate_test_data.py:267:    return coefficients.reshape(cells, -1)

README.md:1:# Postgkyl
README.md:2:
README.md:3:![pytest](https://github.com/ammarhakim/postgkyl/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)
README.md:4:
README.md:5:This is the Postgkyl project. It is both Python library and command-line tool
README.md:6:designed to provide unified access to Gkeyll data together with a broad variety
README.md:7:of analytical and visualization tools.
README.md:8:
README.md:9:## Documentation
README.md:10:
README.md:11:Full documentation of the Gkeyll project is available at
README.md:12:[ReadTheDocs](http://gkeyll.rtfd.io).
README.md:13:
README.md:14:## Dependencies and Installation
README.md:15:
README.md:16:Postgkyl requires the packages listed in pyproject.toml
README.md:17:
README.md:18:Postgkyl requires NumPy >= 2.2.6. In addition, there is one optional
README.md:19:dependency:
README.md:20:
README.md:21:* [pytest](https://pypi.org/project/pytest/)
README.md:22:
README.md:23:[pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/) is required only for developers.
README.md:24:
README.md:25:### Setting up virtual environment (recommended)
README.md:26:
README.md:27:We strongly recommend creating a virtual Python environment for everybody
README.md:28:working with more than one Python project (this includes even using both
README.md:29:Postgkyl and Sphinx). The two recommended options are
README.md:30:[venv](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) and
README.md:31:[mamba](https://mamba.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).
README.md:32:
README.md:33:With `venv`, one can create the virtual environment with:
README.md:34:
README.md:35:```bash
README.md:36:python -m venv /path/to/new/virtual/environments/pgkyl
README.md:37:```
README.md:38:
README.md:39:then activate it with:
README.md:40:
README.md:41:| bash/zsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate`      |
README.md:42:| fish     | `source <venv>/bin/activate.fish` |
README.md:43:| csh/tcsh | `source <venv>/bin/activate.csh`  |
README.md:44:
README.md:45:and deactivate with:
README.md:46:
README.md:47:```bash
README.md:48:deactivate
README.md:49:```
README.md:50:
README.md:51:With `mamba`, one can create the virtual environment with:
README.md:52:
README.md:53:```bash
README.md:54:mamba create -n pgkyl
README.md:55:```
README.md:56:
README.md:57:then activate with:
README.md:58:
README.md:59:```bash
README.md:60:mamba activate pgkyl
README.md:61:```
README.md:62:
README.md:63:and deactivate with:
README.md:64:
README.md:65:```bash
README.md:66:mamba deactivate
README.md:67:```
README.md:68:
README.md:69:Note that with `mamba`, one can also use the provided `environment.yml` file,
README.md:70:which also includes dependency specifications:
README.md:71:
README.md:72:```bash
README.md:73:mamba env create -f environment.yml
README.md:74:```
README.md:75:
README.md:76:### Installing Postgkyl
README.md:77:
README.md:78:The Postgkyl itself is installed with `pip`.[^1] Developers and uses who want to
README.md:79:have the most up-to-date version should install Postgkyl from the source code:
README.md:80:
README.md:81:```bash
README.md:82:git clone https://github.com/ammarhakim/postgkyl.git
README.md:83:cd postgkyl
README.md:84:pip install --upgrade numpy setuptools wheel
README.md:85:pip install -e '.[test]' --no-build-isolation
README.md:86:```
README.md:87:
README.md:88:Alternatively, Postgkyl can be installed directly from [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/postgkyl/):
README.md:89:
README.md:90:```bash
README.md:91:pip install --upgrade numpy setuptools wheel
README.md:92:pip install -e postgkyl[test] --no-build-isolation
README.md:93:```
README.md:94:
README.md:95:#### The Gkeyll bridge (native `.gkyl` reading, `interpolate`, weak algebra)
README.md:96:
README.md:97:Postgkyl talks to Gkeyll through a small compiled bridge (`gpython`), not a path you configure. **This is
README.md:98:built automatically** as part of `pip install`/`pip install -e .`. `setup.py` runs
README.md:99:`scripts/build_gkeyll.sh`, which:
README.md:100:
README.md:101:1. clones [Gkeyll](https://github.com/ammarhakim/gkeyll) into `./gkeyll/`
README.md:102:   (a sparse, blobless, depth-1 clone of just the `core/` app — a few tens
README.md:103:   of MB, not a submodule),
README.md:104:2. `./configure`s and `make core`s it into `gkeyll/build/core/libg0core.so`
README.md:105:   with no external dependencies (`--use-lapack-lite=yes`, so no
README.md:106:   MPI/CUDA/SuperLU/Lua/system LAPACK are required), then
README.md:107:3. compiles postgkyl's `_gpython` CPython extension
README.md:108:   (`src/postgkyl/gpython/csrc/_gpythonmodule.c`) against it.
README.md:109:
README.md:110:This step needs **network access** (to clone Gkeyll) and **a C compiler**.
README.md:111:It defaults to `cc`; if your system doesn't have `cc`, set `CC=gcc` (or any compiler you have) before
README.md:112:installing:
README.md:113:```bash
README.md:114:CC=gcc pip install -e '.[test]' --no-build-isolation
README.md:115:```
README.md:116:
README.md:117:**Always install with `--no-build-isolation`** (as above). Without it, `pip`
README.md:118:builds the extension in a throwaway environment that resolves `numpy`
README.md:119:independently of the one that ends up installed for running Postgkyl. The
README.md:120:extension targets NumPy's `>=2.2` ABI explicitly (matching the `numpy>=2.2.6`
README.md:121:floor above) so that a same-major mismatch fails loudly at import with a clear
README.md:122:`numpy.dtype size changed` error rather than silently — but this is a
README.md:123:best-effort backstop, not a guarantee: a build/runtime NumPy skew has been
README.md:124:observed to crash the native bridge outright (segfault or memory corruption
README.md:125:inside Gkeyll's own C code, surfacing anywhere from the next file read to an
README.md:126:unrelated `matplotlib` call much later) instead of raising cleanly. Building
README.md:127:against the exact NumPy already installed is the only reliable fix, which is
README.md:128:what `--no-build-isolation` gives you.
README.md:129:
README.md:130:If this step fails or is skipped, Postgkyl still imports and works — reading
README.md:131:files falls back to a pure-Python reader, and anything that needs the
README.md:132:compiled bridge (`.interpolate()`, weak `* /` on modal data, native `.gkyl`
README.md:133:reading, `.integrate()`, …) raises a `RuntimeError` naming the missing piece
README.md:134:instead of the pipeline silently doing the wrong thing. Check whether the
README.md:135:bridge is active with:
README.md:136:```bash
README.md:137:python -c "from postgkyl import gpython; print(gpython.available())"
README.md:138:```
README.md:139:
README.md:140:To rebuild by hand (e.g. after pulling a Postgkyl or Gkeyll update, or after
README.md:141:fixing a compiler issue), re-run either script from the repo root — both are
README.md:142:safe to re-run:
README.md:143:```bash
README.md:144:scripts/build_gkeyll.sh   # full: re-clone/build libg0core.so, then the extension
README.md:145:scripts/build_gpython.sh  # just the extension, if libg0core.so is already built
README.md:146:```
README.md:147:
README.md:148:If `gpython.available()` is `False`, the printed error explains which of the
README.md:149:two prerequisites (compiler, or the clone) is missing, or whether the built
README.md:150:extension is stale relative to the shim header — the fix in that last case
README.md:151:is always `scripts/build_gpython.sh`.
README.md:152:
README.md:153:## Testing
README.md:154:
README.md:155:Postgkyl utilizes [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/) for testing. The tests can
README.md:156:be called manually from the root Postgkyl directory simply by using:
README.md:157:
README.md:158:```bash
README.md:159:pytest [-v]
README.md:160:```
README.md:161:
README.md:162:## API and CLI documentation
README.md:163:
README.md:164:Public command documentation lives on the Python function that implements the
README.md:165:operation. The equivalent `GData` spelling is a class-body alias to that same
README.md:166:function, so editor hover help, `help(pg.interpolate)`,
README.md:167:`help(data.interpolate)`, and `pgkyl interpolate --help` cannot maintain
README.md:168:separate descriptions.
README.md:169:The installed distribution includes a `py.typed` marker so language servers
README.md:170:consume these inline signatures and aliases from a virtual environment too.
README.md:171:
README.md:172:Command docstrings use `Args:` entries in Google style. Every CLI-visible
README.md:173:parameter needs one entry; command compilation rejects missing, duplicate, or
README.md:174:unknown parameter documentation. `tests/test_documentation.py` additionally
README.md:175:checks the public Python surface, static fluent aliases, source/runtime
README.md:176:docstring identity, and deterministic CLI lowering. Run it directly with:
README.md:177:
README.md:178:```bash
README.md:179:pytest tests/test_documentation.py
README.md:180:```
